subsubtopic: REFUGEES-GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
Government's refugee policy brings to mind the answer one often hears on the telephone answering service: "Thank you for calling the Government of Canada. Toutes nos lignes sont occupies. All our lines are busy. Veuillez rester en ligne. Stay on the line."
Since February 20 the Government's answer to refugees seeking Canada's protection has been: "Don't bother us, stay home until you hear from us. Don't call us, we'll call you."
The contempt and ignorance of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) are overwhelming. He claims that certain refugees are dishonest because they buy tickets for London but ask for political asylum in Canada. He does not seem to know that a refugee would be putting his life on the line if, before departure, he were to publicize his intention of definitively leaving his country.
Mr. Speaker, February 20, 1987 will for ever be remembered as the infamous day when the Government of Canada broke with our long-standing humanitarian tradition of welcoming refugees.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES PUBLIC MAPPING SERVICES-OPPOSITION TO PRIVATIZATION
DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES PUBLIC MAPPING SERVICES-OPPOSITION TO PRIVATIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time for us to go back to the basics of our language and our principles of government. In the light of recent reports that the Government may sell federal mapping facilities to a private consortium, we evidently have to emphasize that a public
service, the Public Service, is exactly that. It is a service provided to all of the Canadian public.
The mapping services provided by the Government have played an essential role in making Canada a rich, livable and secure country. The services provided by Canada s scientists and our technical mapping specialists are indeed useful to the private sector. They are being shared and must continue to be shared with the private sector.
Vaguely worded statements about joint ventures are not acceptable. A true joint venture, a partnership of independent entities coming together to share skills and opportunities, would not be simply appropriate but essential. But a sell-out of the skills, the technology, and the expertise developed over decades by Canadians working in the service of their country would be a betrayal of government's responsibility to provide a true service to all the people of the country.

subsubtopic: HEARING OF CHILEAN REFUGEE CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Chileans are fleeing brutal repression, disappearance, torture, prison, death, and all the other actions of the dictatorship headed by Pinochet which have been going on for over a decade. There are even secret police in Buenos Aires who are harassing Chileans who are known to be refugee claimants there.
These refugee claimants ought to be allowed to state their claims in Canada under our fast-track procedures and with due process of law. In fact those who have arrived in Canada and have gone through the fast-track procedure have done remarkably differently from the average. The average seems to be about 10 per cent of acceptance of Chileans, it has now become 56 per cent. This shows that they have a strong claim. Even those who may not be precisely refugees by the narrow definition have a strong claim under humanitarian consideration.
There were two planes that left Santiago on the morning of February 20. One arrived in Canada the next day and all the claimants aboard have been accepted. The other one was stopped at Buenos Aires, and should be allowed to come in the same way as the other did with all those who have been accepted.

March 6, 1987

DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES OPPOSITION TO POSSIBLE PRIVATIZATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES
speechtext:

In fact I feel like Premier Peckford and the Hon. Members for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson) and Burin-St. George's (Mr. Price) when they were not informed on the recent Canada-France cod issue. I am beginning to feel more and more like a member of the Opposition.
The Government has enough difficulties these days without looking for more trouble. The potential plan to privatize the Surveys and Mapping Branch of the Canada Centre for Remote Sensing, and the Environment Canada hydrographic services in a joint venture with Lavalin, or any other company in Montreal or Canada, is not only bad business but bad politics. I will fight just as long and just as hard as the unions to prevent this from happening.
If the Treasury Board and the Ministry are flying a trial balloon to see how quickly it gets shot down, well, bang, bang-it's dead!

As
you would know, Mr. Speaker, discussions are now going on in Ottawa in an attempt to bring the Province of Quebec back within the Constitution, with honour and dignity. Sad to say, this is just another masquerade on the part of the Conservative Government because the Quebec Minister of Environment has just stated publicly that his province is being treated unfairly in connection with the St. Lawrence industrial pollution.
In the opinion of the Quebec Minister of Finance, Quebecers are victims of this Government's inequity with respect to equalization payments.
Another Minister, responsible for multiculturalism, is seeking financial assistance from Ottawa to cope with the influx of refugees, and again the federal Government says no.
The Quebec Minister of Transport, Mr. Cote, is opposed to Bill C-18 because it will lead to the abandonment of railway lines in Quebec.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATIZATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES CONDEMNED
DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATIZATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES CONDEMNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked, and so were the surveying and natural resource industries across Canada and the employees at Energy, Mines and Resources, when we learned that the Surveys and Mapping Branch at the Canada Centre for Remote Sensing, and the Canadian hydrographic service are being considered for privatization.
I know the Canadian surveying industry and these government agencies. They are world-class. Industry and government currently interface in a magnificent way. I condemn these privatization initiatives both from a national and local perspective. Many of my constituents work in these agencies, and their careers would be destroyed and their lives disrupted. Nationally, these agencies are regarded as being world class, and that status can only be maintained if they are under the mandate of the federal Government.

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES FOR CERTAIN RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Gerald Bouey, former Governor of the Bank of Canada, did not mince words when he criticized the previous Government for its inflationary policies.
Mr. Speaker, between 1970 and 1984, the Liberals put a hidden tax burden on the neediest in our society, a tax of more than 300 per cent over fourteen years. In other words, Canadians who retired in 1970 with $10,000 in the bank can buy now what they were then able to buy with $3,333. It was the Liberal Party that put this hidden and insidious tax burden on Canadians.
Today's senior citizens who had saved money for their retirement have seen their savings dwindle to only one third of their original value, thanks to the Liberals. And when I see Members of the Liberal Party criticizing our policies, after they robbed Canadians of $7,000 out of every $10,000 over a period of fourteen years-
Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the Liberal Party was Minister of Finance, from 1972 to 1975, he took part in this organized pillaging of Canadians. It was while he was Minister of Finance that we got the 50-cent dollar.
That is what the Leader of the Liberal Party has done for the poor in this country, Mr. Speaker.

DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES REPORTED PROPOSAL RELATED TO PRIVATIZATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Forestry who apparently has charge of the possible privatization of the Surveys and Mapping Branch in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Could the Minister explain what is going on with respect to this proposal for privatization which has led spokespeople for Lavalin in Montreal to talk about plans for employees. They have suggested that not all the employees will be taken over and only two years of job security will be provided. Can the Minister explain what is going on? Could he assure this House and those 1,300 employees in surveys, mapping, the remote sensing centre and the hydrographic service, that their jobs and their work will not be privatized under this Government?
Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of State (Forestry and
Mines)): Mr. Speaker, first I would like to point out that the media reports on this particular matter are incorrect. I want to state at the outset unequivocally that we will not be selling the Surveys and Mapping Branch. I want to tell the employees of that branch in Ottawa, the people of Ottawa and the people of Canada, that that branch is not for sale. Neither are there plans to privatize that particular branch. In fact we have never discussed privatization in the strict sense of the word.
I do want to mention that through recommendations of the Nielsen Task Force, Treasury Board officials are looking at ways in which the private and public sector could complement each other in domestic and international markets for that particular service. However, in this regard Treasury Board and EMR officials have had exploratory discussions with a number of companies, not just one company. I think it is important to note here that Ministers have not in any form considered the policy related to these discussions. Media and Lavalin statements go well beyond what is warranted by these exploratory and preliminary discussions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
That this House, alarmed by the role of air-launched Cruise Missile deployment in violation of SALT limits and alarmed by threats to the integrity of the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, aware also of the possibility of a negotiated elimination of all medium-range nuclear missiles in Europe, calls for strong initiatives by the government to strengthen arms control and disarmament measures including the termination of Cruise Missile testing in Canada.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I urge all Members of the House to support this motion. I feel it is particularly timely that we should do so, as the motion itself suggests. I wish to refer to it in a little more detail than was possible when writing the motion.
I think that all Members of the House in all three Parties are alarmed by the role of the air-launched Cruise missile and its deployment in violation of SALT II limits. Indeed, last June the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) protested the breaching of SALT II limits which would come about if the United States put the one hundred and thirty-first Cruise missile-equipped strategic bomber into place. Our Secretary of State for External Affairs protested to the American Secretary of State, and I believe he protested to the President.
Members of our Party, the Liberal Party, and other parties also said that one of the most important bulwarks of our security, and the common security, was the maintenance of arms control regimes. Nevertheless, at the end of last year, the United States administration, through the deployment of the one hundred and thirty-first strategic bomber, did breach the limits of SALT II.
This is particularly important for Canada, and for Canadians, because it is we who test the air-launched Cruise missile. The breach of the limits on those bombers carrying air-launched Cruise missiles made us directly complicit in the breach. That is why we called then for giving notice of termination of our testing program.
I do not exaggerate when I say that all Members of the House believe, as the Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations believed, that defence, security, and arms control are all links in a single chain.
Referring to the second clause in the motion, about this time all of us became alarmed. I may say that above all the Government became alarmed about the threats to the integrity
Supply
of the ABM Treaty. These threats came about because of breaches in that Treaty by both sides, but particularly by the potential testing, development, and even possible deployment of the Strategic Defence Initiative, star wars.
All along the Government had said that it would accept research into star wars, that research was prudent. But I understood that at no time did the Government support the testing and development of strategic defences, let alone deployment or partial deployment of those defences. Although I cannot say for sure, presumably the Government made it as clear to the United States as it did on the breach of SALT II limits that it did not wish to see the testing, development, or deployment of strategic defences.
I assume it stressed that such testing, development, and partial deployment that is now taking place, at least as far as the testing and development is concerned in the United States, is a matter of grave concern because it will totally undermine the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. Again, this is a matter of particular concern to Canadians.
If, as Secretary of Defense Weinberger particularly suggests, the research, testing, and development have proceeded so rapidly that there could be partial deployment of SDI by the early 1990s, one of the grave effects of this will be to encourage the Soviet Union to strengthen its strategic offensive weapons, including a much larger increase in the development of strategic bombers carrying air-launched Cruise missiles.
This puts Canada in an incredibly quixotic position of continuing to test air-launched Cruise missiles under an SDI program being pursued by the United States, leading directly to the Soviet Union, which has not hitherto had strategic bombers and missiles as a strong element in its offensive forces, developing that element. We literally invite them to do so.
All Members of the House have been conscious of this since the threats to the ABM Treaty became visible, and the abandoning of the strict interpretation of the Treaty became clear. All of us have realized that the consequent and additional consequent results of this would be to encourage the Soviet Union to develop not only its bombers, but all of its strategic offensive forces.
This brings me to the third element in the motion, which is our awareness of the possibility of a negotiated elimination of all medium-range nuclear missiles in Europe. We are, as is the Government, and the Liberal Party, very heartened by what is taking place right now in the approach toward what is basically a zero option in Europe. It looks very clear that this will be achieved. We do welcome it strongly and heartily. But it will be for nought if, through the violation of SALT II limits, and through the destroying of the ABM Treaty by the development and deployment of star wars, all we are doing is enhancing the threat that comes to both sides by the development of strategic offensive weapons.

March 6, 1987
Supply
The elimination of medium-ranged nuclear missiles in Europe will only enhance, if these other developments continue, the build-up or the escalation of strategic weapons. This is one reason we have always called for and hoped that intermediate range and strategic weapons could be dealt with in one basket and, indeed, that space weapons could be included in that basket.
That has not come to pass. The Soviets have decided that they would go along with separating out the baskets. However, as I say, eliminate intermediate range weapons, nuclear missiles, and enhance strategic offensive weapons, submarine-launched strategic bombers and land-based missiles, and the agreement on intermediate-range weapons becomes enormously weakened.
As I understand it, both the Liberal and Conservative Parties have always argued that the two-track decision taken in 1979, which allowed for the deployment of nuclear missiles in Europe at the same time as arms reduction negotiations were taking place, linked Canada into that decision by making one of our contributions the testing of the air-launched air missile. By the way, that was not the position of this Party. We fought and argued that the testing of the air-launched Cruise missile was strictly an arrangement between Canada and the United States.
It seems to me that the Conservative Party has said all the right things on SALT II and on the ABM Treaty, but it has not made enough criticism of testing development and possible deployment of star wars. It has said many of the right things. It has said that it has urged the United States not to breach treaties. It has urged it to go ahead with the Soviet Union on arms reductions. However, it has not given a clear message to the United States. It has not made it clear to the United States and to the Soviet Union that Canada's security is involved in all these matters, as well as the common security, or that it is in our security interest that SALT II limits be maintained and that the ABM Treaty not be breached.
It is in our interest, as much as the interests of the rest of the world, that we say clearly to the United States that we will not be a part of these breaches, that we will not be a party to seeing an enormous escalation in offensive strategic nuclear arms, and that we will not be a party to developing even a further potential battle of strategic bombers armed with Cruise missiles and now, apparently, Cruise missiles which are called "Stealth" missiles with stealth technology. We have not said this clearly enough. However, more important, we have not taken the one action open to us which would enable us to stop treating our security as a spectator sport and to do something about it, namely, to say that we will not continue participating in this escalation, in this breach of treaties.
However, let us take the argument used by the other two Parties. I referred the other day to a statement by the then Secretary of State for External Affairs on July 15, 1983, when the decision to test the air-launched Cruise missile was made, that this testing was an obligation and a commitment which would be carefully re-examined if progress were made in the other branch of the famous two-track decision, namely, the reduction of nuclear missiles on both sides. That is exactly what is taking place today.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that whether we would now terminate Cruise missile testing was hypothetical until we see what happens in Geneva. However, what I was asking was, since it is becoming clearer every day that the elimination of intermediate-range nuclear missiles is definitely coming, and both sides welcome it, surely we can say today what was strongly implied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in 1983.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
If one reads the words of Senator MacEachen, knowing how to read him-and I have had long practice in he very clearly implied that the reduction of intermediate range weapons would cause us to reassess the situation in respect of air-launched Cruise missiles. At the very moment there is a further strong argument for Canada to take the lead and to say that this is the time-if ever the time were to come it is today to say that we will not continue with testing the air-launched Cruise missile.
It is not enough just to say that we adhere to arms control regimes. We must show that we adhere to them. We must show that we want other nations to adhere to them. We must show that when threats to them or when the dismantling of such arms regimes involves us directly or indirectly, as it does in continuing to test the air-launched Cruise missile, we will take action. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) goes to meet the President at the next summit, or when the President comes here, or when the Prime Minister goes to the Soviet Union in a few months time, he would then be able to say that Canada not only gives lip service to arms control and disarmament measures but Canada practises them.
I should think that the Liberal Party as well is moving in this direction very strongly. I was very heartened to see the Liberal Party at its meeting in the fall pass a resolution asking for the termination of Cruise missile testing. I know it did that in the context of the breach of SALT II, in the context of the threats to the ABM Treaty, and in the context of possible negotiations being reached for the reduction of arms in Europe. Then the defence critic for the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), who at our last motion on Cruise missile testing on June 14, 1983 was one who abstained on our motion as an indication that he was not happy to vote against it, said a few days ago that the time had indeed come to terminate the testing of Cruise missiles. I was heartened when the critic for external affairs, a few days after that, in a statement he made on February 27 also agreed that the time had come, for many of the same reasons that I have been outlining today, if not for all of them, to terminate the testing.
March 6, 1987

I know their Leader has not yet said that, but his Party and his two chief critics have spoken.

speechtext: The Leader will speak.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
The Leader of the Liberal Party will speak. I urge upon them, and upon the Conservatives too, that Canada___all of us in all three Parties-should send a real strong
message, not just say that we are concerned about the arms control regimes, not just say that we fear the development of strategic offensive weapons which may become even greater than they are today, or not just say that we want to see both sides strictly adhere to the ABM Treaty. As I mentioned, we must take the one element of all these matters which touches upon Canadians most directly, most intimately, and most forcefully-the testing of the air-launched Cruise missile-and say that we will not any longer be complicit or involved in the dangers of the dismantling or potential dismantling of treaties.
All of us in the House believe in arms control. We have all said it many times. The public believes very strongly in it and continues to register in favour of terminating the testing of the air-launched Cruise missile. Editorial opinion-and I refer to the Vancouver Sun, for example-is moving in this direction as well. In fact, a clear statement was made that now was the time.
With all the strength I can muster, I want to urge everyone to look at what has been happening, to look at the hope which is building up in Europe, and to look at the two sides of the equation-arms and arms control. I want us to look at what is in our own security interests as well as in the common security, of the interests of all. I want to look at all those things with as much seriousness and urgency today in this debate that I can possibly muster. We want to see Canada act as well as talk. The Canadian public wants to see us act. The message we would give to Washington and Moscow it seems to me could be the strongest possible message there is, namely, that Canada will no longer test the air-launched Cruise missile.

speechtext:
I want to say at the outset that no Party in this House has made a greater contribution
Supply
over time to the cause of peace and disarmament than the Party that I have the honour of leading. I need not recite the accomplishments on behalf of peace and disarmament of the late Lester B. Pearson, particularly in his support of the founding of the peacekeeping role for Canada in the United Nations, or the efforts of Mr. St. Laurent in a similar vein and, in recent years, of my predecessor as Leader of our Party, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, particularly his peace mission and doctrine of suffocation in disarmament. I am proud that I have the honour of continuing his declaration of our opposition as a Liberal Party to the doctrine of star wars and participation by this country in any extension of the Strategic Defence Initiative of the United States. We will continue to monitor the Government of Canada as that whole issue develops.
We have, therefore, from this corner of the House a great tradition in the pursuit of peace. We shall live up to it and we shall continue it.

We do not want peace based on fear and escalation of the arms race.

We want, however, a secure peace with balanced and verifiable reductions in the arsenals of devastation, a peace based on a common understanding and respect of our legitimate requirements for security. This is why we have traditionally and historically looked to security as a road to secure peace. This is why the Liberal Party has been insistent on the maintenance of Canadian security.
In this House Mr. St. Laurent when he was Minister of External Affairs proposed in 1948, when we were all plunging into a cold war, the creation of a "collective security league"- those were the words he used in this House to give the western democracies what he called a preponderance of moral, economic and military force".

This proposal was the beginning of the Atlantic Alliance. This collective security system, which turned out to be a vital factor in maintaining peace, and has been for forty years, has served us well thanks to its fundamental objectives which are the pursuit of peace and our collective security. We have always met our commitments to our allies in these two respects.

Security means that we can exercise our sovereignty in peace over our own land and waters. Without it we would be like tenants without a lease, perhaps in peace for a time, but vulnerable to abusive visitations by friends and foes alike. We have learned our lesson from history. We will not sacrifice our sovereignty and security for elusive goals. We shall make them concrete instruments in the pursuit of peace.
The motion tabled by the New Democratic Party this morning may be well meaning in its broad objectives inasmuch

March 6, 1987
Supply
as it urges the Government to grasp with a vision, that it has so far singularly lacked, opportunities for disarmament and improvements in East-West relations. At long last there are hopeful signs of progress, Mr. Speaker. I shall in a timely way state the views of my Party for these exciting prospects in the opening of the relationship signalled by Mr. Gorbachev's initiative and by the response to that by the United States.

However, the motion before the House today, whose purpose is to sell the policy of the New Democratic Party which is opposed to NATO, is a disappointment to Canadians. It shows once again that the New Democrats have failed to recognize the importance of this country's security and the importance of our vital relationship with our allies.

The motion for that reason is not acceptable to us because it does strike at the heart of NATO's collective defence. It would commit us, we believe explicitly but certainly implicitly, to unilateral disarmament and neutralism for Canada, the course to which my Party cannot subscribe. I intend, therefore, to table an amendment to the motion which would remove these flaws. The words "the role of' at the very beginning of the motion are indicative of the thrust of the motion.
Indeed, when the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam was talking about the air-launched Cruise missiles, it was clear that she was not only talking about the violation of SALT, she was also talking about the very existence of those air-launched Cruise missiles as a deterrent to themselves. In her vocabulary this morning there is a linkage in her mind, and the significance to us is that with these words the motion rejects the fundamental element on which NATO deterrence is based. Mutual deterrence, however much we regret it, is the instrument by which both East and West are now currently maintaining peace. If we reject the role of the air-launched Cruise missile in deterrence, we work for the destabilization of what is already a pretty unstable system of security between East and West. The motion, therefore, has a fundamental anti-NATO thrust which the New Democratic Party is promoting with a complete disregard for Canadian security to our allies who subscribe, as we do, to the need for deterrence until we have put into place a better way of managing the preservation of peace.
With our amendment, the House would express its alarm at the violation of SALT limits by Cruise deployment. We fully share this concern. We are equally concerned with the maintenance of the ABM Treaty which reference is appropriately made in the motion, but we would cast the motion within the mould of our treaty obligations. Our amendment consists, when I present it, of adding at the end of the motion the following wording "in a manner compatible with Canada's NATO and other bilateral obligations".
The agreement under which the Cruise is being tested was entered into by a Liberal Government. We permitted testing in an act of solidarity with our NATO allies in order to carry out
collectively the reaction of the alliance to an escalation of nuclear confrontation in Europe by the U.S.S.R. with the deployment of its SS-20s.
This NATO decision was known as the two-track decision, and the Hon. Member has made reference to it, because in addition to deployment by NATO of a counterforce, it promoted negotiations with the U.S.S.R. for the elimination of all intermediate-range ballistic missiles in Europe by NATO and the U.S.S.R.
The Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam is against the two-track system. She should recognize that in effect, with the reopening of negotiations between the Soviet Union and the United States, we have now again in the current context a re-establishment of the two-track style, and anything Canada does ought to be consistent with that philosophy. Recent U.S.S.R. proposals and U.S.A. responses create new hopes that such negotiations can successfully be concluded.
We intend to ensure that any termination of Cruise testing in Canada is made with full respect to our obligations. Our agreement with the United States provides for such determination in circumstances over which we remain the sole judge, but surely after consultation with our allies. We should not lose sight of the fact that the obligations to which our amendment refers concern the pursuit of peace as well as the maintenance of security. We shall want to terminate Cruise missile testing as a contribution to disarmament negotiations. Therefore, we clearly look forward to concrete results in the negotiations between the two superpowers. The timing of any such termination should further and enhance the pursuit of those negotiations.
I might say that in the pursuit of peace, the Liberal Party does not need any instruction from the New Democratic Party. At our November convention, my Party voted for a cessation of Cruise missile testing. It also voted strongly in favour of Canada pursuing peace through the NATO alliance, and together these are the thrusts of the amendment we will put to the House. Without this amendment, the motion as it stands is not acceptable to the Liberal Party.
There is a distinct difference in our approach. On the basis of its responses and resolutions that are binding upon it, the NDP is a neutralist, isolationist Party. The Liberal Party is not. We are committed to our alliances, we are committed to Canada's international obligations and we intend to continue to move toward ensuring peace by strengthening arms control and disarmament within the scope of those alliances, within the scope of those obligations and within the scope of what those obligations mean to Canada.

An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage, is out of order.

Hon. Members realize that the way to express their disapproval of a motion before the House is to vote against it rather than to propose an amendment which is in fact a direct negative.

The Chair has declared the amendment in order. I simply want to indicate to you, Mr. Speaker, that this Party intends to remove the camouflage, to vote against the amendment, so that the Liberal Party of Canada will have the opportunity to stand in the House of Commons and indicate directly where it stands on this issue. I expect it will vote 40 different ways.
I am pleased these issues are before us. I appreciate the initiative of the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) in bringing the matter before the

House. These questions are of fundamental importance to the country. Some of her comments I could agree with. In that respect I would hope the debate would be regarded by our allies and by others in the country, if for no other reason than to indicate the extent of the concern in this House and in this country about the limited and restricted interpretation of the ABM Treaty.
I must say to the spokesperson for the New Democratic Party that I think this debate also reveals a fundamental difference, not just of substance but of approach to some of these issues between her Party and the Government. There is no doubt of her sincerity. However, I believe she has fallen into what is perhaps an inevitable trap for Parties which are never in office. She thinks it is enough to express opinion. She is not interested in trying to influence events. This Government has the obligation, not simply to express our opinion but to try to influence the events in the world of which we are a part. We are convinced that one does not influence events by opting out. What this motion proposes is that Canada opt out of some of its obligations and opt out of the capacity to have influence on fundamental questions.
This resolution suggests that to support unarmed Cruise missile testing in Canada is to oppose to SALT II. That is false. This motion suggests that Canada could strengthen the West's negotiating position by breaking the western solidarity which helped bring the Soviet Union to the table. That, Sir, would be foolish. It would have the opposite effect. If the New Democratic Party intends to be taken seriously, it should treat seriously these fundamental issues raised in this question.
Let me go through the motion piece by piece. First, this Government fought at every opportunity the U.S. decision to break out of the SALT II limits. We lost the fight. We think the break-out is bad for arms control. However, the fact that the United States does not consider itself bound to an unratified treaty should not lead us to break a signed agreement. We lost an argument on SALT II. The NDP now proposes that we should also lose our influence in NATO, in other words, lose our ability to win any other arguments on issues vital to Canada and to world peace. That, Sir, is not strategy, it is spite. It is not logic, it is visceral anti-Americanism.
Regarding the integrity of the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, Canada is very worried about the consideration being given by the United States to adopting a broad interpretation of the ABM Treaty. As the House will know, the U.S. position to date has been that while a broad interpretation is allowable legally, it has agreed to abide by a restrictive interpretation. Canada supports a restrictive view and we urge the United States to adhere to it.
Yesterday, Ambassador Paul Nitze spoke with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) and myself and heard that view reiterated strongly by Canada. Mr. Nitze made it clear that the United States has taken no decision to move to the broad interpretation. Certain Americans are urging a broad interpretation. They have not yet won the day. The consultations with the
allies, of which Mr. Nitze's visit yesterday was part, is designed deliberately to give an opportunity for those of us who favour a restrictive interpretation to make our case. Those consultations will continue. Canada will continue to make the case for a restrictive interpretation. We will do that in contacts at every level with the United States and in the alliance.
Our view is that, particularly in a period when there is renewed hope for progress at Geneva, it would be wrong for one of the superpowers to unilaterally change one of the existing elements of arms control. We understand that it is a question of legal definition. We understand that the United States has long argued that the broader interpretation is legally correct. We hope we can make enough Americans understand that a change now from the restrictive to the broad interpretation would be a real change in the atmosphere of arms control and, in our judgment, a change for the worse.
Again I ask the House, how do we best influence the Americans? Does our influence increase if we break our agreements with them regarding the testing of the unarmed Cruise? Of course, it does not. There is a chance, even a good chance, that the combined weight of the allies, speaking with unity, can persuade the President to continue to adhere to the restricted definition of the ABM Treaty. The New Democratic Party wants us to break that allied unity. That would mean losing the best chance we have to work effectively for a restrictive interpretation of the ABM Treaty.
Third, the INF talks mark a very important, indeed, a very exciting breakthrough. Mr. Gorbachev has taken an important initiative in dropping his insistence that SDI and intermediate nuclear forces be dealt with together. We welcome his stepping back from that condition in the same way we welcome the tabling in Geneva by the United States delegation of a draft treaty proposing the complete elimination of U.S. and Soviet INF missiles in Europe. This treaty reflects longstanding alliance positions as well as drawing on important understandings which were reached at the Reykjavik Summit. It is the embodiment of an ambitious plan for the elimination of a whole category of missiles in Europe, a plan, Sir, which was developed in concert with the alliance over a period of several years. Taken together, these two actions by the superpowers represent a positive and encouraging step.
Very important questions remain. There will be serious problems of verification. There is the question of what to do with the short-range missiles in Europe not included in the discussions now engaged in again at Geneva. There is the question of the placement outside Europe of the remaining intermediate nuclear forces and, undoubtedly, as the negotiators in other countries scrutinize the language of Mr. Gorbachev's proposal, and scrutinize the language of the U.S. draft treaty, other serious questions will also arise.
The point to underline, however, is that arms control negotiations have begun again in earnest. It is important for us both to reflect upon how that happened, how it came to be and also to consider what it might mean. Obviously, it came to be as a result of several factors, including imaginative and
March 6, 1987

courageous decisions by leaders of both the superpowers, but in the longer perspective it is undeniably the case that a major factor leading to these arms control negotiations has been the consistent unity displayed by the allies of the United States. There has, of course, also been unity on the part of the allies of the Soviet Union. They have no choice. Allies in a democratic alliance have a choice. Every time that choice is exercised there is the opportunity to break alliance unity or to respect alliance unity.
There are widely different views within the North Atlantic Alliance. Part of the Soviet strategy consistently has been to try to bring those differences into the open, to try to break the unity of the western alliance, because the Soviets knew that divisions in the West would weaken the hand of the United States at the negotiating table.
One of the major reasons, Sir, we have the prospect of an arms control agreement today is that the West has stood together. Yet, in this House of Commons, on the eve of the resumption of serious discussions of an INF agreement in Europe, we are being invited to break that western unity which helped bring both sides to the negotiating table. The motion of the New Democratic Party is an invitation to set back the arms control negotiations process. We have seen the skill, particularly in recent months, of the Soviet Union in dealing with western opinion. Imagine what it would do with a decision by Canada on the eve of INF discussions to break an agreement respecting the testing of the unarmed Cruise missile. That would be broadcast everywhere as evidence of division in the West, as evidence of weakness in Washington. Instead of leading to serious discussions it could unravel the serious intent that has been demonstrated so far.
One of the reasons we are so active in this alliance is that we believe that alliance unity makes progress on arms control possible. Progress on arms control is very important to the Government and to the country.

speechtext:
I for one do not propose to throw away the prospect of arms control progress because of erratic resolutions that might have been taken at a political party convention of the Liberal Party or of the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, suppose we consider another aspect. An agreement on intermediate nuclear forces would affect the land-based cruise missiles that contribute to Europe's nuclear deterrent capacity. The cruise missiles being tested in Canada under an agreement with the United States are air-launched and are part of the strategic deterrent forces of the United States. The role played by U.S.-based strategic deterrent forces in maintaining the global balance of nuclear deterrence would expand if an INF agreement were to lead to the elimination of U.S. missiles in Europe. In this perspective, tests
Supply
to verify the reliability and effectiveness of air-launched cruise missiles would be needed even more if an agreement on intermediate nuclear forces were concluded, both from the point of view of arms control and defence.

One of the Government's priorities in our arms control and disarmament policy is the enhancement of strategic stability. The air-launched Cruise missile with its long flight time and its relatively slow recallable carrier is currently among the most stabilizing elements of nuclear deterrent forces. However, we believe that it too should be subject to arms control restraints. We have supported the inclusion of air-launched Cruise missiles in the limits on strategic nuclear arms being negotiated at the Geneva talks. But those decisions should be made by negotiations at Geneva; they should not be made unilaterally, disruptively or individually for reasons of spite, ideology or the dictates of a Liberal or NDP convention.
The Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam spoke earlier about Canada's security being involved. Of course, Canada's security is involved. We are not here involved in an empty debating forum; we are here involved in a common alliance trying to come to terms with some of the most difficult and stubborn questions ever to face mankind. They are critical questions. They are vital questions. If we do not resolve them, they could literally mean the end of us all. We have an obligation to do the best we can to exercise every ounce of influence that we have. Influence is not exercised by taking actions of spite that cut off ones obligations. One does not help people get to the negotiating table and then, just when the hard negotiation is about to begin, weaken the side which one supports. That is not the way for people to work in an alliance. More important, that is not the way for us to achieve progress on arms control.
The Government and the country have a distinguished record in this regard. I was interested in the observations of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition who paid deserved tribute to the late Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson for the roles they played in trying to bring about understanding in control of arms to the world. We are continuing to play that role. We are trying to return Canada to that tradition of constructive participation, influencing our allies, working with our allies toward constructive progress. That is the position of the Government.
We have spoken and acted on a number of fronts. Sometimes our arguments carry; sometimes they lose. But if we are serious about this we cannot run away in spite every time we lose an argument. What we have to do is stay and fight so that our arguments have a chance to prevail.

The point I was making is this. Somehow it is not divisive of the alliance, according to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for Canada to oppose the United States breach of the SALT agreement to which they had adhered for a number of years. I know that it was not a treaty. It is not divisive of the alliance for Canada to oppose the broad interpretation of the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has pointed out, that is something that Canada has done with force and vigour on a number of different occasions, both publicly and privately. It is not divisive of the western alliance, and of our friendship with the United States and the other countries in NATO, for Canada to refuse to support the star wars or the Strategic Defence Initiative. That is all right, too. The Secretary of State for External Affairs did not criticize it, so presumably he accepts that it is all right for other NATO countries to have a differing view of their obligations, to refuse to have foreign troops on their soil, to have a different command structure relative to troops which they have loosely committed to NATO, or to refuse to have testing of nuclear weapons or placement of nuclear weapons on their soil. That is all right, too. But then the Secretary of State for External Affairs has turned around and said that it is not all right if Canada takes the step that we have proposed, which is that we should simply refuse to have testing of Cruise missiles in Canada.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is saying, as the Liberal Government said before him in 1983 and 1984, that there will always be reasons for the Government to defer action on Cruise testing. There will always be reasons to refuse to act, and to refuse to stop Cruise testing despite the opinion of the majority of Canadians who say that it is time to stop testing of Cruise missiles in Canada, and that that time is now. It is because of the way that we as Canadians feel about what
March 6, 1987

our role should be in the world, and about the type of contribution that we can make to world peace and disarmament.
The New Democratic Party has the view that the amendment proposed by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is contradictory to the motion. However, you have accepted it as being in order. We are not prepared to vote for the amendment proposed by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition because it is definitely contradictory to the motion which is being debated today. Our motion makes it quite clear that we call for the termination of Cruise missile testing in Canada, not in five years, 10 years, some indeterminate time, not depending on whether it is February, March, or November, but that we do so now.
We do have a bilateral agreement with the United States. Under that agreement we have a sub-agreement relative to Cruise testing. In other words, at the present time we are committed to Cruise testing. However, there is a loophole in that agreement which, in view of substantial changes in the international situation, permits us to say, let us stop Cruise missile testing in Canada now. We are saying that now is the time to invoke that particular clause. We do not have to wait until July, 1988, or until 1992 or 1993 when the umbrella agreement expires. We can do so now. We should do so now. That is the message that clearly should be taken by the House voting for the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett).
In moving the amendment stating that the resolution would be supported only in a manner that is consistent with Canada's bilateral obligations, I believe we have what is known as an oxymoron; it is a contradiction which is in fact not sustainable. That is why we are not prepared to support the Liberal amendment. I am glad to hear from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he, like us, is prepared to see this issue clearly debated and discussed in the House with a clear vote in terms of Canada's taking the initiatives in the area of disarmament and arms control, and on the specific question of whether we should stop Cruise missile testing, and stop it now.
The New Democratic Party has always been opposed to Cruise missile testing. I would point out that these tests are not being made in the context of Canada's obligations to NATO. In fact, they have not been requested by our friends in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. They have been requested under the umbrella agreement which exists with the United States. These tests are to add to the American strategic forces and, as my colleague has already pointed out, these forces now exceed the SALT limitation in terms of bombers capable of carrying air-launched missiles.
The level of strategic forces is already too high and too dangerous on the side of both superpowers; 10,000 more missiles is ample for the western allies to obliterate the Soviet Union and its friends, I suppose some 400 or 500 times, and I believe for the Soviet Union to do the same thing to us here on the North American Continent. Frankly, once is too many times. Twenty, 50, or 200 times beyond that is far too many.

We are particularly concerned about the Cruise missile because it is destabilizing, and because it is of particular danger to us in Canada with the most sparsely populated terrain which lies in the field of potential conflict, should there ever be such a devastating conflict between the superpowers.
One of the concepts of deterrence which has lasted for 35 years, albeit imperfectly, is that each side has some knowledge of the level of weapons, and the threat which is directed against it by the other side. In fact, by various means the two sides do seek to inform each other of what they have, and to know what the other side has. In other words, there is not total secrecy in this area, and there is a certain common interest in knowing what they have pointed against each other. Therefore, it is crucial that weapons be detectable.
The Cruise weapon deters detection because it cannot be seen, traced, or tracked as easily as conventional strategic missiles. The Cruise missile deters arms controls and verification because it is so small. Something that will fit on the back of a tractor-trailer cannot be verified. There are probably hundreds of thousands of tractor-trailers in this country, and millions in the United States. Any one of those could purportedly be carrying beef, furniture, or some other product, or it could be carrying two or three Cruise missiles that potentially could be used against some potential adversary.
This matter should be of particular concern to Canada. Since taking office the Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated in his statements that Canada is committed to arms control in the context of deterrence. If there is a weapon which, if widespread, undermines deterrence, we should be doing our best to discourage it rather than allow its proliferation.
It has been argued today by the Leader of the Official Opposition that to stop Cruise missile testing would violate the two-track concept of the European NATO policy which has been pursued for the last several years. Regardless of one s views on that particular policy, it is a fact that the air-launched Cruise missile is not an intermediate weapon. Therefore, it is not part of that two-track policy which was directed to the European theatre.
The air-launched Cruise missile is designed to go over the North Pole, down the rivers of Siberia, and to hit inland centres in the Soviet Union without being detected at an early point in any type of strategic or hideous exchange between the superpowers. It was not called for, and it has nothing to do with the two-track policy of NATO. There is no NATO obligation with respect to Cruise testing in Canada.
We have no agreement with NATO in respect of Cruise testing. We have an agreement with the United States. As the Hon. Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) and the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau, at the time they were responsible Ministers in their respective Governments, admitted in the House that there is no NATO obligation.

However, they are only biding their time. The President has not abandoned his commitment to his interpretation of the star wars initiative, which would require a broad rather than a narrow interpretation of the ABM Treaty, and which, therefore, threatens to undermine the only arms control treaty in force between the United States and the Soviet Union.
Also, as my colleague pointed out, there was a dramatic prospect for the removal of all intermediate range missiles in Europe. I do not believe that we as Canadians should be encouraging a new area of competition between the superpowers, just at a time of taking away a particular area. I profoundly believe that the removal, or an agreement to remove intermediate nuclear force missiles, coupled with the progress made on chemical weapons, the progress made on conventional troops in the Stockholm Talks, the progress being made at the United Nations in terms of unanimous support for Ambassador Roche's resolution or Canada's resolution on verification measures related to nuclear testing, and the lengthy moratorium to which the Soviet Union adhered, despite the failure of the United States to go along with it, are surely reasons to seek a pause in the escalation of the ludicrous nuclear competition which has taken place for many decades between the superpowers.
We have therefore presented a motion that attempts to enable Canada to take an initiative that reflects Canadian public concern and will be a valuable contribution to arms control and to nuclear disarmament. As a NATO member, I would point out that Canada is free to choose the manner of its contributions to NATO. Various NATO countries do not allow foreign troops. They do not allow nuclear missiles on their borders. They have different means of interpreting the treaty. Even if there were some loose form of NATO obligation, there is not a specific obligation. The suggestion about a
bilateral obligation is there, but let us spell out exactly what it means.
We have an umbrella agreement on testing with the United States. Regrettably the Government chose last week to do nothing about that agreement and, therefore, it is extended from 1988 to 1993. Cruise missile testing takes place in the context of that over-all agreement. It is in the context of the sub-agreement that we have the opportunity either to continue or to cease. We do not believe the bilateral obligation is sufficient to outweigh Canada's commitment to maintaining the integrity of the ABM treaty, to maintaining the SALT agreement, and to ensuring disarmament and mutual security.

Mr. Speaker, the long-standing position of the New Democratic Party has been to oppose cruise missile testing in Canada. On behalf of Parliament, we ask all parties here in the House of Commons to oppose cruise missile tests in Canada right now, and not to defer or muddle the decision but make it clear.
I welcome the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that the Government will vote against the amendment of the Official Opposition because indeed we must have a clear vote. We on this side welcome the fact that it will be a clear vote, and we appeal to all political parties to side with the majority of Canadians who want to see an end to the cruise missile tests and hope Canada will take a new initiative aimed at world-wide disarmament.

With that being said, I find that the motion itself does contain a number of serious ambiguities, some of which were addressed by my leader in his comments at noon. It certainly wants from lack of precision, as we have just heard from the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) who read the word "now" into the text, which it does not have. Should we give the NDP the benefit of the doubt, that this is simply bad drafting, or is there something more mischievous about this motion? For example, as the leader pointed out, the very first line of the motion attacks the role of air-launched Cruise missile deployment. This morning in her opening comments, the sponsoring member said, again changing the language of the motion, that the House is alarmed by the role of air-launched Cruise missiles and the violation of the SALT limits.
I heard her say it right here. It is the intention of this motion to attack the role of air-launched Cruise missiles, which was the point raised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) this morning? He made the point that that is a direct assault on the deterrent factor of NATO itself. It appears to me that the New Democratic Party is trying to bootleg an attack against NATO and the deterrent effort of NATO through this resolution, in a very cute way.
As far as the violation of SALT II is concerned, we have expressed our concern. I will come back to SALT II in a moment. I know the New Democratic Party has expressed concern about those violations and representations that have been made to Washington, and made in the conference of NATO Ministers as recently as in Halifax, but their concerns
seem to have fallen on deaf ears. The breach of those SALT II limits has become a symbol in this arms race, and its deliberate breach suggests that there are now no limits. That is a matter of great concern to us on this side of the House. I will return to SALT in a moment.
Those words, "the role of', used in the context with which they were put forward this morning, add nothing at all to that motion, unless they are designed to attack NATO itself and the deterrent NATO feature. If one eliminates those words, I suggest to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, who is nodding his head, that, yes, indeed the point with respect to SALT II limits is still there.

The New Democratic Party we know rejects Canada's role in NATO and NORAD. It has not had the courage to say so directly in this resolution. I hope that the amendment proposed-I hope adopted-will make the New Democratic Party honest on this point, so it will say here in this House where it effectively stands.
Turning to the last sentence of the motion, that which calls for the termination of Cruise missile testing in Canada, it is interesting to note that once again, the resolution falls far short of precision. However, it is not unlike the resolution which was adopted last November at the Liberal convention. Following that convention, our Leader explained that the resolution was to be interpreted within the context of Canada's bilateral and multilateral commitments, notably to NATO. The amendment he has moved, which I have seconded, brings precision to this motion. I urge all Members of the House to accept it notwithstanding the rejection of it out of hand by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in his intervention earlier this afternoon.
On February 27, in fact one week ago, I had called for an arrest or stop to Cruise missile testing, as I had on earlier occasions in the House. For example, on December 1, 1986, as reported on page 1643 of Hansard, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs the following question:
Could the Prime Minister advise President Reagan that Canada does not intend to proceed with the Cruise missile tests until the U.S. Government decides to meet its obligations under the SALT II Treaty and the ABM Treaty?
Like others on all sides of the House, across Canada, in the United States and in Europe, I have been concerned by the apparent obdurate attitude of the United States on at least three issues, and I will deal with them, which directly affect arms negotiations because they seem to be preventing the implementation of the most important track of the two-track policy adopted back in 1979. I do not intend to deal at great length with history, but we should bear in mind that, as we have already heard, the two-track decision was to deploy nuclear weapons on European soil on the one hand while seeking to pursue arms reduction negotiations at Geneva on the other.
March 6, 1987

As the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) pointed out, in 1983 our Government entered into a test and evaluation agreement with the United States, and subsequent thereto the United States asked Canada to test Cruise missiles. It was terribly important at that time, as it is today, that there be solidarity in the Atlantic alliance as these negotiations with the Soviets were approaching.
The Cruise missile decision was not an easy one to make, but within the collective solidarity of the alliance, European nations were agonizing over the requirement that they place nuclear-armed missiles on their soil. Canada agreed that to fulfil its role and to do its part, it would test unarmed Cruise missiles in this country. I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to a letter addressed to the Hon. George Shultz from the then Secretary of State, the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, of July 15, 1983. He said:
You will recall that when I wrote to you on January 21, I underlined the serious concern of the Canadian people about the decision their Government might take on the anticipated U.S. request to test the cruise missile in Canada. At that time I stressed how important it was for the Government to be able to assure the Canadian public that the arms control aspect of the negotiations in Geneva is being pursued as vigorously and as earnestly as is the deployment of new missiles.
He went on to point out the following:
Canada joined in the NATO "two-track" decision in 1979, under which new Allied missiles will be deployed in Europe beginning this year unless a verifiable agreement can be reached with the Soviet Union to make this action unnecessary. When we met with our NATO colleagues in Paris in June we agreed that, if the negotiations are to succeed, it will be important for all the Allies to stand together behind their decision. As our contribution to this solidarity, Canada has agreed to help test vital components of the technology of the cruise missile.
The two tracks were clear: the deployment, of which the testing of the Cruise missile was a part, and the renewed effort to secure arms reductions. The arms-reduction track has not proceeded as the world might have hoped, but Mr. Gorbachev's arrival on the scene brought new hope for meaningful arms reductions. The security track, of course, has been followed very well. However, Mr. Gorbachev threw out the challenge to get back on that other track when he said: "On behalf of the Soviet people, I am appealing to the wisdom and the dignity of the Americans not to miss another historic chance on the way toward ending the weapons race".
I think many of us felt that the United States administration did not adequately accept that challenge. First and foremost, there was the star wars initiative. That, as we know, suggested that there would be a broadening of the interpretation of the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. This interpretation, if agreed upon by the United States, would presumably allow extensive testing and deployment. I must say I was heartened to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell us today that Paul Nitze, the senior arms adviser to the President, has told the Canadian Government that the United States has not yet moved to that broad interpretation. Nonetheless, that is a matter of great concern.
The second issue which prevented us from getting back on that second track was the failure to accept a moratorium on nuclear tests, something which had been offered by the Soviet
Supply
Union and which had in fact been followed by the Soviet Union for 18 months. The reason, of course, the moratorium was not accepted by the United States was that it apparently was intimately related to this ill-conceived star wars initiative. Apparently nuclear testing is necessary to develop one of the essential components of that system, the nuclear X-ray laser.
Third, we saw the breach of the SALT II limits against the wishes of all the NATO allies. The Secretary of State made the point that they argued with great vigour in Washington to convince the United States not to breach the SALT II limits. However, on all these issues, the moratorium, the reinterpretation of the ABM Treaty and the SALT II limits, the Americans did not appear to be listening to our concerns or to the concerns of the allies. All of our pleas seemed to fall on deaf ears.
The result of that was that arms-control negotiations, for which we had so much hope after the arrival of Mr. Gorbachev and the initial meeting in Geneva, were, all of a sudden, the subject of dismay and despair because of what I call this apparent obdurate attitude on the part of the United States. Negotiations came to a virtual standstill.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that at Reykjavik, Mr. Gorbachev insisted that the removal of the intermediate-range nuclear missiles in Europe depended upon the abandonment of the star wars initiative by the United States. However, the seemingly stubborn refusal of the U.S. to make concessions on star wars prevented the pursuit of meaningful negotiations in that regard. We seemed to have lost that most important track of all, namely a concerted, solidified and consolidated effort on the part of the allies to sit down and negotiate an arms control agreement with the Soviet Union.
How do we get back on track? The U.S. did not seem much impressed with our rhetoric, our arguments or those of our allies. The star wars and SALT road-blocks remain. That is why I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs last December 1 whether he could advise the President that Canada wanted to discontinue Cruise testing until the Americans started to live up to their obligations, as we saw them, under the ABM Treaty and SALT II, notwithstanding the fact that SALT II had not been formally ratified. What has happened? Since I last suggested that course of action and a discontinuance of Cruise missile testing, Mr. Gorbachev has changed his position and attempted to place the arms reduction negotiations back on track with negotiations on the removal of intermediate-range nuclear weapons from Europe. I am gratified and pleased to see that the U.S. has in turn made a solid and positive response. This may indeed be the historic breakthrough. During this period, I suggest, the allies have to stand solidly together because the purpose of the interventions I made in the past was to get them back on track and it now looks as though we are getting back on track. I would like to refer to the comments of two respected journalistic sources in

Canada. In an editorial on March 3, The Globe and Mail, referring to Mr. Gorbachev and the zero option, said:
He has thereby opened the way to the first major arms control pact of the 1980s.
I would also like to refer to Mr. Richard Gwyn who writes a column for The Toronto Star from London. It is a sensitive, perceptive and informed column. He offers the following comments:
Gorbachev has done it. Because he has done it, almost anything now becomes possible: A major cut in long-range (intercontinental) missiles that would free both superpowers from their fear of a surprise attack; elimination of chemical weapons; phasing out of nuclear tests, and a pact to reduce conventional forces.
Much is left to be done, but Mr. Gwyn adds optimistically, and I would like to share some of that optimism:
The catalytic new agreement Gorbachev has added to East-West relations is that of trust.
The U.S. and the Soviet Union are moving back to the table. As you know, on March 4 the U.S. handed the Soviet Union a draft treaty agreement. Obviously I have not seen its terms, but we understand it would eliminate all medium-range nuclear missiles in Europe and limit the two superpowers to 100 nuclear warheads apiece of the same kind of missiles on their own soil. On the eve of these negotiations which could begin that historic breakthrough, and which will hopefully move into other areas of disarmament such as ICBMs, chemical warfare and tactical nuclear weapons, I would not fire off a message to the U.S. that we are going to terminate our relations under that agreement. That was the point that our Leader made this morning and that is the point I would make to the gentleman from Ottawa Centre. I do not see that as enhancing these negotiations when we must stand solid because we finally are back, it would appear, on both tracks. We finally can see real opportunity for major breakthroughs on arms control.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), has very clearly laid out Canada's position on the very important area of arms control and disarmament. He has done this, as he said, at a time when some small rays of sunshine have appeared in what has been a gloomy arms control environment of late. The Department of National Defence has been pleased to lend support to recent efforts in this field.
Canada's position on arms control and the value of existing treaties is clear. Arms control is a very important aspect of national security, but so is defence.
In the short time available to me, I hope to demonstrate that the defence aspect, including such activity as testing the Cruise missile in Canada, is a necessary and valuable adjunct to the arms control effort.
For many years now, the western alliance strategy of deterrence through strength has helped us avoid a major East-West conflict, including the ultimate horror of nuclear war. The major component of deterrence from the western viewpoint has been provided by nuclear weapons, the vast majority of that nuclear deterrent being provided by the United States.
A strategy of deterrence requires that the weapon system components of that deterrent be viable. This viability can only be ensured by the testing of systems, continually upgrading them in keeping with developing technologies, and demonstrating that viability to friend and potential foe alike.
It is a fact that the Soviets, and their Warsaw Pact allies, continue to upgrade their air defence forces. Their interceptor aircraft, surface to air missiles, surveillance systems and the command and control facilities to co-ordinate all of this are of a very high calibre. The ALCM helps to balance the equation.

March 6, 1987
Supply
Ensuring the viability of a component of deterrence is not in opposition to a viewpoint that supports arms control. In fact, the opposite is true. Viable deterrent systems encourage arms control. It is in that context that Canada is following its version of a two-track system, that is, supporting testing and evaluation of a component of the nuclear deterrent while actively encouraging progress in arms control. There is no contradiction in our approach.
Canada's defence is inextricably linked to the policy of collective security arrangements with the United States and our European allies. In this way, Canada is able to make a unique and valued contribution to enhance alliance security. These arrangements are very much linked to the nuclear deterrent strategy I mentioned earlier. They go hand in hand.
Our contribution might be seen as modest compared to those of other NATO allies who have nuclear weapons deployed on their territory. Some of those weapons are the subject of current debate and, provided the right guarantees come to pass, may be removed in the future.
The point is that it was the resolve of the alliance to deploy these weapons which has allowed the West to negotiate from a position of strength rather than a position of weakness.
The European allies took bold and difficult decisions which may now begin to bear fruit. Should Canada do any less? Of course not.
The decision to test the ALCM in Canada recognized the need within NATO to share the burdens and obligations of collective defence. That need has not changed. In fact, as potential breakthroughs in arms control appear, alliance solidarity is more necessary now than ever before. In addition, close co-operation with our allies, particularly the United States, ensures that we do have a voice at the bargaining table. The strategic defence of North America is a joint responsibility, and we must ensure that our views are heard. Canadians do not want their Government to abdicate its responsibility in this regard. There is more to be lost than there is to be gained.
An argument frequently heard against the air-launched Cruise missile is that it is a first strike weapon and it is therefore destabilizing. Any serious strategist knows that this is simply not true. ALCMs must be carried to their launch points by bombers. Given the large number of bombers required to mount an effective first strike and the long flight time to reach those launch points, it is very likely that any enemy would have ample warning. This warning time would be extended by the long flight time of the Cruise missile itself. Total surprise could not be ensured by air-launched Cruise missiles, and no prudent military planner would risk launching an attack in that manner. I hope that will set the record straight.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the United States Air Force has just completed two very successful test flights of the Cruise missile in Canadian air space. Those flights not only proved
the effectiveness of the system but also allowed for some very useful collateral training and research by the Canadian Forces. The CF-18s of our air defence force were given the opportunity to practise intercepting and tracking the Cruise missiles. Other valuable research work was done in surveillance and defence against the Cruise missiles such as giving our CP-140 Auroras an opportunity of verifying their detection systems.
Hon. Members will be aware of the recent increases in the number of Soviet long-range bombers approaching the Canadian air defence identification zone. The bomber known as the "Bear-H" is a Cruise missile carrier. Just as the Cruise missile itself is part of the deterrent, so are the forces which defend against Cruise missiles. Thus, Cruise missile tests in Canada provide a very useful training vehicle for our forces.
In replying to this motion, I should remind the House that the project arrangements for Cruise missile testing is part of an over-all test and evaluation agreement with the United States. This agreement was signed by the previous Liberal Government in 1983. There have been misleading reports recently in the media in regard to a so-called extension of the agreement. Those reports have left an impression that the Government is committed to a further five years. This is, of course, not the case. Once again, let me set the record straight. The agreement was for an initial five-year period with an automatic five-year renewal. The agreement has always been, and still is, liable to termination at any time by either party giving 12 months' notice. Furthermore, it can be terminated at any time in an emergency. Either party can terminate a specific arrangement under the agreement-for example, Cruise missile testing-at any time on one day's notice should imperative circumstances so warrant. The Government is not held captive by this agreement. We have repeatedly stated our intention to carry on, and will do so, but this in no way precludes second thoughts should circumstances change.
In order to maintain the strength of deterrence, a program of test and evaluation is vital. Making our territory available under sound and safe conditions is a valuable contribution by Canada to the western alliance. Canada benefits from the protection provided by the nuclear deterrent. We also benefit from the opportunity to practise and improve our own air defences in conjunction with the Cruise Missile Test Program.
In closing I would like to say that there is no contradiction in supporting a reasonable and meaningful commitment to a stronger defence effort, and yet being equally supportive of peace initiatives. In my opinion, the twin concepts of peace and security are inseparable. I take great pride as a Canadian in associating myself with our Prime Minister's view that "we are not a nation that has any international aspirations except that of peace". May we always continue, as a nation, to pursue that aspiration.
