speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is sad to hear the word games which have taken place today in attempts to wriggle around particular clauses and to escape from the basic question which is before the House. That basic question is one which has to be put perhaps by a new generation of Members of Parliament.
In the past months and weeks I have received letters from Brownie packs in my constituency. These are heartfelt letters, letters written by little girls who want to say to us assembled here as Members of Parliament that they want peace in the world. They want to grow up. They want to have good and productive lives ahead of them. They want to see Canada become a leader in the fight for peace. We have received letters from seven or eight different Brownie packs in Windsor.
I can read some of the letters which represent typical ones which have been sent to us. I think it is crucial that Members of Parliament hear some of the words sent by our young citizens, people such as Lindsay, who is six, who writes:
Ask Prime Minister Mulroney to talk with President Reagan about peace and getting rid of nuclear weapons.
Others have written to us and stated: "I think Canada should help find a peaceful solution to the problems causing war". Those words are from Laura who is seven. "Canada should help other countries to find peaceful answers to their problems." Those are the words of Bonnie who is six. This is very much the voice of a generation that has a sense of fear, because there are those of us who, frankly, have let them down in the last 10 to 15 years.
It seems to me that there has been case after case of potential peaceful initiatives put forward in terms of steps which could take the world from a dangerous path of escalation in arms and in its capacity and willingness to use arms, to a path of de-escalation and disarmament. These are initiatives that will take us away from the possibility of what could be a nuclear termination of civilization as we know it. That is basically what this motion is about today. It is not a motion about scoring partisan points, or embarrassing one Party or
another; it is a motion that is setting front and centre before the Parliament of Canada at least two or three of the crucial issues which are wrapped up in the arms control debate.
I have been very disappointed by the recent actions of the Government with respect to this cry from our young people for a peaceful world. For instance, I heard today from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) about how we must be inextricably linked to the alliance system, as if the alliance system were an end in itself. Surely the goal is to achieve a peaceful world and establish a momentum toward disarmament. If the existence of alliances stands in the way of that, they should be dismantled and not extolled, as was the case with the last speaker from the Government.
This crazy approach that has been suggested here, in the United States, and also in Margaret Thatcher's Britain, that somehow through strength we will get peace makes me think more of George Orwell and the reversal of meaning of the words where the ministry of war becomes the so-called ministry of peace. That is what we are talking about when we hear the Government and leaders from the western alliance talk about the goal of peace through strength.
In the last year and a half we have seen the destruction of SALT II. It was supposed to be a movement toward strength, yet it destroyed one of those basic elements of stability which remained within the world. In spite of that, the United States continued to deploy its Cruise missiles and overstep the bounds which existed within the SALT II agreement.
Let us look at the spectacle of a Government in the United States which has admitted that it lied to its own people. It is now sending its representatives throughout the world and is trying to persuade us, the allies of the United States, that we should reject the ABM Treaty as it was established in 1972. Again, that was one of the basic points of stability, one of those few threads that saved us from further escalation in the potential for nuclear war. Let us talk about Reykjavik and what appeared to be an agreement which was reached and very quickly repudiated by the United States.
Let us talk about the initiative taken by the Soviet Union to put a ban on nuclear testing. We may have thought that this was some type of trick on the part of the Soviet Union. But surely anybody who looked with care at what was taking place had to come to the conclusion that this was a sincere gesture that suggested to us that if the United States responded there could be a nuclear test ban treaty. Yet that too was rejected.
With the type of steps that have taken place in the past year and a half, it is time for us to recognize reality and to recognize that the thrust throughout this period has been toward escalation, and not toward disarmament. Running implicitly through that thrust is the tremendous amount of resources that have been allocated by the United States to the Strategic Defence Initiative within the United States, and the nibbling effects and attempts by the United States to circumvent the
March 6, 1987

ABM Treaty and to put in place some elements of that SDI system for testing purposes. That is what has taken place.
Yet Canada stood aside while this has gone on. Our words have been good. I previously mentioned to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that I was pleased that the decision was taken not to put Canada into SDI as a full partner. There were steps taken to say to the United States, not out of spite or out of anger or adolescent retribution but as part of a serious effort on the part of this country, that we wanted to put into effect the commitment of our young people, our Brownie packs and those girls who have written to me from Essex County, and the commitment that we heard right across this country from the joint special committee which looked at our international relations. In city after city we heard from peace groups that had come together in the middle of the summer under difficult circumstances and said to us, as passionately as they possibly could, "We want Canada to be a peacemaker. We want Canada to be a leader in the fight for peace. We want Canada to challenge those who are not prepared to give their priority to a peaceful world for the future".
That challenge has not been taken up. With the case of Cruise missile testing, a simple, easy, and straightforward message could be sent to the United States, without great cost to that country, without great cost to the alliance system, or without great cost to United States' thinking or its overwhelming concern about security. A step could be taken. Cruise missile testing could be stopped easily. It could be stopped at once, which would have an effect. The effect would not be to stop the arms race. The effect would not be to cause immediate changeovers in American thinking from escalation to disarmament. It has taken, instead, some quite creative and courageous gestures on the part of the Soviet Union-and I am not afraid to say so-to take that direction in the future. It has also taken a much weaker President within the United States looking for ways to respond, to get the direction of change finally shifted. It could have been helped. It could have been assisted. We in this country could have given it a little push. We could have listened to young people across the country who have talked to us in heartfelt and very deeply concerned terms. We could have said no to future Cruise testing.
If we had done that, it would have helped. We could have taken, as our motion suggests, a much more critical position vis-a-vis the United States in respect of its attempts to overstep SALT II. We could have taken a much more argumentative position in respect of the ABM Treaty in public than we have done thus far. We could have taken those steps.
In doing that, we would have made the contribution for which our young people are asking. I am referring to the contribution believed in very strongly by the generation that came after World War II and that believes that any future war will destroy the world. I hope not just this Government across

I urge my friends on all sides of the House to take the opportunity provided by the resolution, which strongly expresses the passionate concern of our young people, to put their voices and votes behind the resolution and to give it support, not as a panacea or a final answer, but as something which will help change the dangerous escalation of the present to what I hope will be the disarmament of the future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
Of course, the Speaker is right as he always is. It does not matter ultimately at the end of the day who said no. Let me only say, as I am entitled to, that it is with great regret that I heard from whichever direction I heard it, but my left ear picked it up best, the "no" that was shouted out because I was looking forward to hearing finally from a member of the New Democratic Party indeed what the Party's position was with respect to Canada's obligations under NATO and other bilateral treaties.
There is an interesting phenomenon in Canadian politics. In Canada, we have a system of the two traditional Parties which have put forward policy, postulated on the solutions to the problems of the nation at any given point in time, and engaged in vigorous debate while a third Party has sat on the sidelines with a pea-shooter in an attempt to score quick, easy, cheap points. In recent days, for whatever reasons-and I won't go into them-this Party has found itself with a slight surge in the public opinion polls. Today is as good a time as any for Canadians to begin to ask themselves what it is this Party stands for.
For far too long, Canadians have taken the view that it does not really matter what members of the New Democratic Party stand for because they will never be in a position to do anything about it anyway. They do not look that closely at what it is they stand for because Canadians have traditionally taken the view that the NDP has a Utopian view of the planet, everything for everybody, a carrot for everyone, and what they stand for is not really that important. Unfortunately, this Party picked a Friday to move this motion, a day not traditionally known as one for a great membership in this place. They picked a moment when the Leader of their Party could not be here. One must understand that he had other more pressing and realistic engagements to attend to.
I said a moment ago, and it ought to be restated, that as much as I as a Liberal disagree with my friends opposite about unemployment initiatives, I must believe that as human beings, they care fundamentally about the unemployed. They may be awfully stunned about how they are trying to cure the problem, but I have to believe they care. As much as I may be concerned about peace on this planet and as much as I may believe from time to time that their policies are not the right ones, I must believe that they care about every man, woman

and child in Canada. We may agree to disagree on how we come to grips with many of the problems we face, be they social, military or economic, but all of us are here perhaps pursuing different policies but ultimately trying to achieve the same objective.
What I find offensive-yes, offensive-about the motion put forward by the member of the New Democratic Party is that it was almost blinding to watch members of the New Democratic Party deliver their presentations on this motion because the effect of the haloes they were wearing would nearly knock your eyes out, Mr. Speaker, It is the holier-than-thou attitude that says: "We can create in this nation an island apart and separate from the rest of the planet earth, and because, having carved a trench so deep and wide around this nation that the rest of the world does not matter, we can speak out, send out our message, express our Utopian vision and the rest of the world will listen". It is that kind of naive, narrow quality that emanates from members of the New Democratic Party that is either the function of a childlike, beautifully innocent view of the world, God bless them, or a kind of insidious simplifying of complex issues in an attempt to attract votes. It is one or the other, either a childlike beauty in their thinking, and may they retain it for a long time, or a deliberate attempt to grab the polls on any given day and say they have a policy to solve world problems and express it by way of resolution in the House. I suspect it is the latter.
The fact is that every Member of Parliament wants to see an end to Cruise missile testing in an appropriate fashion within the context of our obligations under NATO and NORAD and to our partners in the western alliance. It is not beyond the realm of possibility, if we go beyond the stereotypes painted by members of the New Democratic Party of Conservative or Liberal Members, that in the appropriate context, even the Conservative Party would find an appropriate moment to end Cruise missile testing when it makes sense in the context of our obligations. However, this motion sets Canada up as some widget existing on some unknown planet that has no neighbours, alliances, organizations or treaties to worry about, and that is not reality. That is why the Liberal Party moved a very simple amendment to the motion of the New Democratic Party about which members of the New Democratic Party claim they care. It was an amendment that said that disarmament measures including the termination of Cruise missile testing in Canada should be taken in a manner consistent with our NATO and bilateral obligations.
If members of the New Democratic Party were sincere and meant what they said, if they were serious about convincing more people in Canada to look at grasping the opportunity when appropriate to end Cruise missile testing, they would support the Liberal amendment that was put today because it does not negate their motion. It merely asks that we grow up and recognize that we are not an island unto ourselves. It is an amendment that asks that we recognize that we are full players in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It is an amendment that asks that we recognize that we are part of the
NORAD agreement, and one that asks that we recognize the nature, reality and history of the planet earth, as imperfect as it is, on which we live. That is all it is. It is an amendment that proves that we are now out of the university debating club and into the House of Commons, a part of the real world that takes us beyond fantasy. That is all it is. We asked the NDP to support that amendment. Yes, all Members of Parliament want to give voice to their desire to achieve a safer world. However, our actions have to be more than empty words and rhetoric. They have to be meaningful. To be meaningful they must be taken in the context of our obligations to NATO and our neighbour to the south.
There is something which occurs in this place far too often and it troubles me. Some Liberals and Conservatives are guilty of this, but it is primarily Members of Parliament from the NDP who have a hard time making a distinction between a disagreement with U.S. policy on any given day of the week, and expressing an overwhelming and general dislike for the U.S. No one can be brought to his feet faster in a fit of frustration than this hon. servant from Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe when a tariff is put on fish. No one can express quicker his frustration and anger when cedar shakes and shingles, softwood lumber and countless other products are harassed by the U.S. administration. However, I make the distinction between U.S. policy on trade or, for that matter, any other area, and my frustration and anger at that policy, and my sentiments about my neighbour, that nation south of the border. Too few members are making that distinction. We have heard the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) say he is not one of those who believes that the U.S. is some kind of sleeping giant being run by a Goldfinger in the back room. I am glad to hear that because too many members of his caucus have and express that view.
The motion before us as amended expresses the concern of the House with the role of the air-launched Cruise missile and its deployment as a violation of SALT limits. The motion expresses the concern of the House about the integrity of the ABM Treaty. It calls upon the Government of Canada to adopt stronger measures to protect the integrity of SALT II and the ABM Treaty, including cancellation of Cruise missile testing within Canada's obligations as a member of NATO and under our other bilateral treaties. That is the amended motion before the House. I submit that every single Member of Parliament can and should be able to support it. I say that not only to my friends in the NDP, I say it to Members of the Conservative majority. It merely expresses the will of this Parliament to use all of those vehicles at our disposal, within the bounds of our responsibilities and obligations, to try to play a role and exert some influence in this world. The words we have added to the motion remind us of our obligation and take us back to the real world. Canada is but one of many players. We like to believe, as we sit in this place enraptured by the splendour of our chandeliers, television lights and stained glass windows, that this is the only Parliament on the planet. The
March 6, 1987

NDP would say that this is so. Everywhere around the world people are tuned to what is being said in the Parliament of Canada and there are no other voices and no other Parliaments. All we have to do is but to speak and megamillions stand up and applaud. Well, that is not the real world. That is not the planet we live on. That is not the way it works.
Unless this nation is prepared to play its role in the treaty organizations we belong to, we may as well abstain from the international arms debate. That is what the NDP would have us do. That is its policy as spelled out at its convention and spelled out by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor today. The NDP believe the best way that Canada can have a say and exert influence is to withdraw from NATO. Let Canadians from coast to coast hear that. That is its policy. It is also its policy that we withdraw from NORAD. The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor has said it for the first time, I think, in years in this Parliament.
The reason this motion is put before the House today and the reason the NDP has rejected our amendment is that that Party wants to make this House and its members turn Canada into an isolationist, pacifist nation of philosophical angels wandering about in the clouds miles above what is really happening down here on the planet. It is a wonderful place we want to preserve, but it has some warts, and wishing them away will not make them disappear. I beseech members to support the Liberal amendment to this motion

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Hon. Member for his statements about the NDP. He was very clear and direct, and I want to thank him. I would also like to ask him where he thinks that Party places its faith. The NDP certainly does not place it in our NATO or NORAD allies. Perhaps it places it with the other side, the Soviet Union. That regime would not permit a man suffering from cancer for over six years to leave that country. How can we possibly trust a regime like that in disarmament talks when we cannot trust them to follow the basic human rights accords they have signed? If the NDP does not put its faith in the teamwork of democracy, where does the Hon. Member think it is placing its faith?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question and comments, although I suspect I may disappoint him slightly. You have to believe one of two things about members of the NDP. Either they are as childlike in their view of this world as they portray themselves to be and are genuine about it, or they are very Machiavellian. I do not believe they can possibly be that Machiavellian, so I assign to them a childlike beauty in their view of the world. I would not want to suggest, as the Hon. Member might lead me to suggest, that the NDP would put its faith in the Soviet Union. I would not want the Member to believe, despite my comments about the NDP, that I think the role for Canada is to follow in a slavish manner the lead of the U.S. Nor should we follow in a slavish

manner the lead of the U.S. Nor should we in a slavish manner always condemn the Soviet Union. I think the role for Canada is to take an independent course, to be slavish neither to our NATO allies, nor to be bound in some doctrinaire way to suspect or condemn always the initiatives of the Soviet Union. Our role is to stay in the game, as frustrating and as tough as it is. As angry as we may get on some days with our NATO partners, we can only have a role to play if we are in the game.
The New Democratic Party motion and its policy to get out of NATO and NORAD and set itself up as the high priest of honesty and integrity is the equivalent of myself, the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe, not being satisfied that I am heard properly in this place, going to a mountain top to talk to myself and be satisfied because no one disagrees with me. The NDP would have us go to the mountain top, talk to ourselves and listen with pleasure to our own echoes because no one disagrees with us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ARMS CONTROL-CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext: I rise today simply to say to members of the New Democratic Party that if they are serious about this motion and making progress, they should lend support to the amendment put by my Leader which would ask us to play a mature and responsible role in the world. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have one question for the Hon. Member. What is his position and the position of his Party on Cruise missile testing in Canada? Does he support nuclear weapons and the original agreement that was introduced by Mr. Trudeau in the last Parliament?

McGuil, who protested against the Cruise missile tests and wanted her protest put on the record of the proceedings of the House of Commons. The same afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I received nine telephone calls. Not many perhaps, except that even a single protest in my riding is important and deserves consideration.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about armament or disarmament, we are tempted to consider every possible solution under the sun, and I think everyone wants to have the widest possible range of solutions open to public scrutiny.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I am against capital punishment, but that does not mean I want to see murderers walking down Main Street. That this House, alarmed by the role of air-launched Cruise Missile deployment in violation of SALT limits and alarmed by threats to the integrity of the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, aware also of the possibility of a negotiated elimination of all medium-range nuclear missiles in Europe, calls for strong initiatives by the government to strengthen arms control and disarmament measures including the termination of Cruise Missile testing in Canada.
In amendment thereto Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra), seconded by Mr. Johnston, moved:
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end of the motion to a comma and adding the following: "in a manner consistent with Canada's NATO and bilateral obligations".
The question is on the amendment. All those in favour of the amendment please say yea.
